transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my primary care doctor actually insisted I come see you. It’s been a whole ordeal, to be honest. Everyone’s just making such a massive fuss about my weight lately, saying it’s dropped too low and all that. My sister even called me three times last week just to ask what I was eating, which, frankly, is exhausting. But I keep telling them—and my doctor, who wouldn't really listen—that being this light is actually a good thing for me. I’m a carpenter, you know, and I’m 59, so I’m not exactly a spring chicken anymore. Being lighter just... it helps me keep up with the physical demands of the shop. I’m on my feet all day, lifting wood, moving around, and when I weigh less, I just feel so much more agile. I don’t get bogged down or feel heavy and sluggish like some of the guys I work with. I mean, I can still out-work half the people in there, and I really attribute that to not carrying around any extra bulk. It’s just practical, really. But my doctor saw the scale and just panicked, I guess, and now here I am, taking time out of my day to talk about something that I honestly feel is helping me, not hurting me. I just don't want to get slowed down, you know? And this is how I manage that.
Do you think your current weight is normal for someone of your age and height?

Normal? Well, what even is normal anymore? If you look at the average person my age, they can barely get up a flight of stairs without losing their breath, let alone haul lumber around all day. So, no, I guess I’m not 'average' normal, but I think my weight is perfectly fine for me. It’s actually getting quite frustrating because my husband keeps harping on it. Every single evening when I get home, he looks at me with this overly concerned expression and says I look too thin, always hovering and asking if I’ve had enough to eat, which just drives me completely up the wall. 

And it’s not just him, unfortunately. It’s bleeding into my work now, which is where I really draw the line. The apprentices at the shop—these kids who are barely in their twenties and still don't even know how to properly square a joint without me holding their hands—they actually have the nerve to chime in and tell me I look too thin! I mean, I’m the one teaching them the trade, I'm the one running circles around them on the floor, and they’re analyzing my body. I just keep telling them all that I’m fine. Because I am fine. 

Honestly, I really think people today are just confusing discipline with sickness. Just because I have the willpower and the strict routine to keep myself lean and efficient for my work, suddenly everyone thinks there’s something wrong with me. They see someone who doesn't overindulge, someone who actually controls what they do so they can stay sharp and light on their feet on the job, and they panic. It’s not a sickness to care about your physical efficiency and keep yourself in working order, you know? It’s just discipline. But nobody seems to understand the difference anymore. They just see that I don't look like every other fifty-nine-year-old and jump to all these crazy conclusions without actually looking at how well I'm functioning.
Do you think you look too thin?

Well, no, not at all, but like I was just saying—my husband and those kids at the shop, they certainly seem to think so. It’s like a broken record with them. I get home, and my husband gives me that look, you know the one, like I’m about to just snap in half if the wind blows too hard, and he says, 'You look too thin, you need to eat more.' And then I go to work, and it’s the apprentices. These kids, I swear, they should be focusing on the wood grain and making sure they don't lose a finger on the band saw, but instead, they’re looking at me, telling me I look too thin. It’s just so inappropriate, honestly. 

But I just keep telling them all the same thing: I am absolutely fine. I look fine. I look like someone who takes their job seriously. I really believe that what they’re seeing—what they’re all calling 'too thin'—is just them confusing discipline with sickness. They look at me, and they see someone who doesn't have an ounce of extra fat slowing them down, and because they don't have that kind of willpower themselves, they assume it must be a disease. It’s like, if you’re not soft and slowing down by the time you’re sixty, people think there’s a problem. But I look in the mirror, and I see someone who is streamlined. I see a body that is built to work, not to sit around. So no, I don't think I look too thin. I think I look exactly how I need to look to do what I do, and I just wish everyone else would stop projecting their own lack of discipline onto me and let me get on with my life and my work.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Well, afraid is a strong word, but... yes, I suppose I am. I mean, it’s not an irrational fear, it’s just practical, like I’ve been saying. But it does get into my head. For instance, if I even think about eating anything heavy—like, say, a big bowl of pasta or a heavy stew, the kind of things that just sit in your stomach like a lead weight—I start worrying right away. And don't even get me started on holiday foods. My husband’s family has all these rich, butter-laden recipes they pass down, and we used to make them every Thanksgiving and Christmas. But now, if I let myself have even a little bit of that, my mind just starts racing. I start worrying immediately that I’ll gain weight, that I’ll get sluggish, and that I’ll lose the grip I’ve worked so incredibly hard to keep. 

Because it really is a grip, you know? It’s a tight hold on my routine, my efficiency, my whole way of operating in the shop. If I gain weight, I lose that edge. I lose the agility. And the thought of going into work and feeling heavy, of struggling to lift a piece of oak or getting winded halfway through the day... that terrifies me. It really does. I’ve built this whole system to keep myself functioning at a high level, and the idea of ruining it just for the sake of eating something heavy or indulging in some holiday pie... it’s just not worth the anxiety it causes me. So, yes, the thought of gaining weight definitely worries me, because it feels like I’d be losing control over the one thing that keeps me going strong.
Does the fear of gaining weight affect how you go about your daily activities?

Well, I mean, I still go to the shop every single day. I'm not the kind of person who just stays home and wallows, you know? I have a business to run. But... I suppose things have shifted, and it's incredibly frustrating. It's not so much that the fear stops me from going in, but it’s how everything around me has changed because of it, or because of how I’m managing myself. 

Like I said, I have my routine, right? I keep myself light and efficient. But lately, my husband has started showing up at the shop more often. He used to just let me be, let me run my crew. Now, he’s coming by under the guise of 'bringing me lunch' or 'just checking in,' and he’ll just linger. He watches me. And the apprentices—oh, this is the part that really gets under my skin—the apprentices have started stepping in when I go to lift something. I’ll be walking over to grab a stack of two-by-fours, something I’ve done a million times, and suddenly one of these kids is right there, practically elbowing me out of the way, saying, 'I got it, boss, let me handle the heavy stuff.' 

And it’s not just once or twice. It’s a constant thing now. They’re taking over the heavier work, the lifting, the moving of materials, the things that require real muscle. And they do it with this... this look, like they’re handling a piece of fragile glass. It drives me absolutely crazy. I built that shop. I trained them. But now, with my husband constantly hovering and the kids treating me like I can’t carry my own weight—literally and figuratively—the whole place just feels... different. It feels less like my own shop and more like some sort of supervised playground where I’m not allowed on the big equipment. So, yes, I’m still there, I’m still working, but the dynamic has completely changed, and it makes me feel like I’m losing control of the one space that was entirely mine.
Do you restrict what you eat because of your fear of gaining weight?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. But you have to understand the context of it, because it’s not just about, you know, starving myself for the sake of it. It’s about maintaining that efficiency I was telling you about. It’s about keeping the engine running smoothly without clogging it up. 

So, on workshop days, which are most days, I have a very specific way of doing things. I usually just have tea. Hot tea, maybe with a little lemon, because it keeps my hands warm and it gives me something to sip on while I’m looking over the blueprints or checking the inventory. And maybe, just maybe, if I really feel like I need it, I’ll have a few careful bites of something. Like, half an apple, or a single cracker. Just enough to keep the blood sugar from totally bottoming out, but not enough to actually sit in my stomach. 

Because the thing is, stopping for a real meal—like sitting down with a sandwich or a salad, or whatever it is my husband keeps trying to push on me—it just feels completely unnecessary. It disrupts the flow. When I’m in the shop, I am dialed in. I know exactly what needs to be cut, what needs to be sanded, what needs to be assembled. If I stop to eat, I lose that momentum. I start thinking about the food, and then I start worrying about how heavy I’m going to feel after I eat it, and then I’m distracted. And in my line of work, distraction is dangerous. You lose focus for a second, and you ruin a beautiful piece of mahogany, or worse, someone gets hurt. 

So, by keeping it to just tea and a few bites, I keep that control. I keep the day moving exactly how I want it to. It’s a very deliberate choice, you see. It’s not just some random fear; it’s a calculated decision to ensure that I stay sharp, that I stay light on my feet, and that I don't lose the grip I have over the day. If I were to eat a full meal, it would just throw everything off. The control I have over my routine, over my body, over the whole operation—it would all just slip away. And I can't afford that. I really can't.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

Well, that’s exactly why I’m sitting here in this chair, isn't it? My regular doctor—the one I’ve been seeing for years—he’s the one who actually sent me to see you in the first place. I went in for just a standard check-up, mostly because my husband wouldn't stop nagging me about making an appointment, and of course, the first thing they do is put you on the scale. And suddenly, it’s like alarm bells are ringing in the clinic. 

So, yes, my weight has dropped. Apparently, it’s dropped so low that it’s this massive crisis now, and everyone is just making such a huge fuss about it. My doctor was throwing around all these concerned looks, my husband is treating me like I'm made of spun glass, and it is just so incredibly exhausting. They look at the number on the scale and they panic, but they don't live in my body. They don't understand how it actually feels. 

I honestly feel like being this light is exactly what I need. It helps me keep up with the shop! You have to understand, when you're on your feet on a concrete floor for ten, twelve hours a day, moving between the table saw and the assembly benches, dodging materials... any extra weight is just drag. It just slows you down. When I was carrying more weight, I felt sluggish, like I was dragging myself through the afternoon slump. But now? I’m light. I’m agile. I don't get slowed down by feeling heavy or weighed down. I can pivot, I can move, I can get things done with that exact efficiency I was telling you about earlier. 

So, yes, the number is significantly lower, I won't deny that. But to me, it's just stripping away the excess. It’s streamlining the whole operation. I just wish they could see it from my perspective instead of treating me like I'm going to blow away in a stiff breeze. I'm a carpenter, for heaven's sake. I know how structure works, I know how load-bearing works. And right now, my frame is carrying exactly the load it needs to to get the job done, and absolutely nothing more. I just don't see why everyone is acting like the sky is falling when I'm functioning exactly how I want to.
Has your fear of gaining weight affected your relationships with your family or friends?

Well, I wouldn't say *my* fear has affected anything. If anything, it’s everyone else’s bizarre reaction to me that’s causing problems. I mean, I already told you about my husband, right? How he’s constantly hovering around the shop now, bringing me sandwiches I didn't ask for, interrupting my workflow. That’s definitely put a strain on things at home, because we end up bickering about it, but again, that’s him acting out of line, not me. I’m just trying to run my business the same way I always have. 

And as for friends... well, I don't have a massive social circle. You know how it is when you run your own business, you just don't have the time for ladies' luncheons and all that nonsense. But I do have a couple of close friends, women I've known since my thirties. We used to—well, we still do, I suppose—try to get together on Sunday mornings at this little diner over on 4th Street. It's this classic, old-school place, vinyl booths, the works. Anyway, we used to just sit and chat, and now... now it’s like walking through a minefield. 

If I just order a black coffee—which is perfectly fine, their coffee is actually very good, they roast it locally—my friends give each other these *looks*. You know the look? That sideways, tight-lipped glance across the table. And then one of them will inevitably slide a plate of toast toward me or ask in this overly gentle voice if I’m 'feeling okay.' It’s infuriating! I’m sitting there, perfectly fine, wanting to talk about the crazy markup on lumber right now or the supply chain issues we're having with oak, and they’re completely fixated on whether or not I’m going to eat a piece of sourdough. 

So, sure, things feel a bit tense, and I honestly find myself making excuses to skip those Sunday diner trips lately because I just don't want to deal with the interrogation. I'll tell them I have inventory to do, or a custom cabinet to finish up. But I don't see that as *my* issue. I'm just living my life, staying efficient, staying light. They're the ones who have suddenly decided to make my plate the center of every conversation we have. If they could just back off and treat me like the same person I’ve always been, everything would be perfectly fine. So no, I don't think my mindset is ruining my relationships. I think their inability to mind their own business is what's really doing the damage.
Are there activities outside of work that you've stopped doing or avoided because of your fear of gaining weight?

Well, outside of work... I mean, work is my primary focus, as I’ve explained, because when you run your own custom shop, the work really never stops. But, I suppose... yes, there are things. Family things, mostly. The holidays, for instance, are just an absolute nightmare for me now. 

It used to be that I’d host, or we’d go over to my sister-in-law’s place down in the valley, and there would just be this massive, endless spread of food. You know the kind of thing—heavy casseroles, mashed potatoes loaded with butter, the pies, all those rich, dense foods we used to make for every single holiday without even thinking twice about it. My husband's family is big on tradition, so it's the same heavy menu every single Thanksgiving and Christmas.

But now? I just can’t do it. I really can't. I find myself making up excuses to avoid those gatherings entirely. I’ll tell them I have a big commission to finish before the new year, or that I need to do a deep clean of the dust collection system in the shop, which always takes a full weekend. My husband gets furious, of course. He says I'm isolating myself and ruining the holidays. 

But he doesn't understand the panic it causes me. Because if I eat anything heavy, or let myself have the foods we used to make for holidays, I start worrying right away that I’ll gain weight and lose the grip I’ve worked so hard to keep. It’s not just a passing thought; it's this intense, immediate anxiety. It’s like I was saying before about the shop—everything has to be precise. Everything has to be controlled. And sitting at a table full of gravy and stuffing is just so unpredictable. It threatens the entire balance I've built. 

I just know that if I give in and eat it, I'll feel that sluggishness, that heaviness pulling me down, and I'll start putting on the weight I've managed to strip away. I’ll lose my edge. I’ll lose that streamlined efficiency. So, rather than sit there and panic about every bite, or deal with everyone watching my plate, it’s just easier to stay in the shop where I know exactly what’s happening and where I have total control. So yes, I suppose I do avoid quite a bit outside of work now, just to protect that balance.
Do you avoid social gatherings where food is involved because of your fear of gaining weight?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago about the holidays... yes, absolutely. It all ties back to exactly what I was just telling you. Any gathering where food is the main event is basically off the table for me now. I mean, I know I already mentioned my sister-in-law's house, but it really applies to everything. If I eat anything heavy, or, you know, if I let myself have those foods we used to make for holidays or even just a regular weekend dinner party, I start worrying right away that I’ll gain weight. It's this immediate, overwhelming panic that I'm going to completely lose the grip I’ve worked so incredibly hard to keep. 

And it's not just the big family events, really, though those are the worst offenders. It's the neighborhood block parties, it's the summer barbecues my husband's buddies throw... you go to these things and what do they have? Burgers, potato salad dripping in mayonnaise, huge bowls of chips. And people just stand around the grill and eat without even thinking about what it’s doing to them. I just can't be around that environment anymore. I look at those tables and all I can think about is how that food would just sit in my stomach, how it would slow me down in the shop the next day, how it would add bulk to my frame that I absolutely do not need. 

I've spent so much time and effort getting my body to this perfect, streamlined state where I can move around the table saws and the lumber racks without feeling weighed down. Why would I jeopardize that? So, yes, I avoid them entirely. I'll tell people I'm busy with a commission, or I'll just send my husband on his own—which, like I said, he absolutely hates and we argue about it constantly—but I just can't risk it. If I even take one bite of something rich or heavy, my mind just spirals into this terrifying place where I can literally feel the weight coming back on, and I refuse to let that happen. I simply cannot lose that control.
Do you feel like your efforts to maintain your current weight are causing problems in your relationships with others?

Well, again, I really have to push back on the premise of that question. I don't feel like *my* efforts are causing the problems. I feel like *their* reactions to my efforts are what's causing the problems. It's exactly like what I was saying about the diner with my friends, or the holidays with my husband's family. I'm just living my life, running my shop, keeping myself in peak condition for the physical demands of my work. 

But my husband... oh, he just won't let it go. He’s constantly making these comments, telling me I look too thin, telling me I'm wasting away. He’ll come into the shop—which, like I said, he never used to do—and he'll just stand there, watching me sand a piece of mahogany, and he'll say, "You're just skin and bones, it's not right." And it's not just him! The apprentices I have at the shop, these two kids in their twenties who barely know a dovetail joint from a hole in the wall, they've started chiming in too. They’ll offer to lift things for me, or they’ll ask if I need a break because I look "frail." Frail! Me! I’ve been hauling lumber since before they were born. 

I tell them, all of them, my husband, the apprentices, my friends... I tell them I am perfectly fine. I am more than fine, actually. I'm operating at maximum efficiency. I don't have the sluggishness that comes with carrying around extra weight. But they just can't seem to grasp it. I keep trying to explain to them that people are confusing discipline with sickness. That's really what it comes down to. In this society, nobody understands discipline anymore. If you aren't overindulging at every opportunity, if you actually have control over your body and your intake, people think there's something wrong with you. They look at my dedication, my ability to stay streamlined and focused, and they label it as a problem. So, no, my efforts aren't the issue. It's their complete inability to recognize hard work and discipline when they see it.
Are there any activities you enjoy doing in your free time that you've had to stop or reduce because of your concerns about weight?

Free time? Well, I don't really believe in "free time" in the traditional sense, to be perfectly honest with you. My work *is* my passion. Woodworking, designing, building custom pieces... that’s what I enjoy doing more than anything else in the world. It’s not just a job to me, it’s my entire life, my identity. So, I still go to the shop every single day, bright and early, just like I always have. I haven't stopped doing that. 

But... I will admit, the experience of being there has shifted, and it's incredibly frustrating. And again, it’s not because I’m concerned about my weight, but because of everyone else’s obsession with it. Like I was just saying about my husband and those two apprentices... they've completely changed the dynamic of my own workspace. 

I'll be getting ready to haul a stack of oak, or I'll be setting up to load heavy boards into the planer, and suddenly one of them is right there, practically hovering over my shoulder. They've started taking over more and more of the heavier work, insisting they do it for me, treating me like I'm made of spun glass. And if they aren't grabbing lumber out of my hands, they're constantly checking on me. My husband will pop in unannounced, or the apprentices will poke their heads into my office, asking if I need to sit down, asking if I need a break... it's just exhausting. 

I built that custom shop from the ground up. I poured my blood and sweat into it for years. And now... with them constantly stepping in and treating me like some fragile invalid who can't handle her own materials, it just makes the whole place feel less like my own. It used to be my sanctuary, you know? The one place where everything made sense and I had total control. And now I can barely move a sheet of plywood without a peanut gallery analyzing whether I'm strong enough to do it. So, no, I haven't stopped going, but they are certainly draining all the joy out of it for me.
Are there other daily activities, outside of work and social gatherings, that you've changed or avoided because of your concerns about gaining weight?

Well, if you are talking about my daily routine, the actual structure of my day-to-day life, then yes, I suppose my schedule is different now. But I really need to be clear here, because you keep framing it as this... this panicked avoidance of weight, and I keep telling you it is about efficiency and discipline. 

Take my workshop days, for example. Which, let's be honest, is practically every single day of the week for me because I am always in the middle of a build. I used to do the whole traditional routine, you know? I’d stop around noon, brush the sawdust off my clothes, wash up, and sit down for a full lunch. Sometimes I'd even go down the street to grab a sandwich. But I just don't do that anymore. I've completely cut that out of my day. 

Now, on workshop days I usually just have tea. I'll make a large thermos before I leave the house—just plain black tea, or maybe green, nothing added to it—and I'll sip on that while I'm looking over blueprints or waiting for wood glue to set. And maybe, if I'm doing some really intricate detail work and I feel like I need it, I'll have a few careful bites of something. Just a tiny bit, just enough to keep my hands perfectly steady. But that is absolutely it. 

Because honestly, stopping for a real meal... it just feels completely unnecessary. I don't understand why people feel this constant need to interrupt their productivity just to consume things. You stop what you're doing, you put all this heavy, rich food into your system, and then what? You have to try to get back into the rhythm of the work while your body is sluggish and bogged down trying to digest it all. It throws off the entire flow of my work, and worse, it throws off the control I’ve got over the day. I have this perfect, streamlined system from the moment I walk into the shop. I know exactly how my body is going to move and respond. Sitting down to eat a plate of food just shatters that control. I need to stay light on my feet, I need to stay sharp, and my tea gives me exactly what I need without ruining my momentum or weighing me down for the afternoon. So I just skip the whole meal charade entirely.
Do you intentionally try to lose weight or maintain your current weight by restricting your food intake?

Well, "restricting" is such a loaded word, isn't it? It sounds so negative, like a punishment. I prefer to think of it as being highly selective and disciplined about my fuel. But to answer your question... yes, I do intentionally control exactly what goes into my body. I have to. 

Because, if I'm being completely honest with you, the thought of doing otherwise is... well, it's highly distressing. If I eat anything heavy, or if I were to let myself have the kinds of foods we used to make for the holidays—you know, my husband's family always expects these massive, rich spreads, the butter-soaked potatoes, the heavy gravies, the dense pies that just sit in your stomach like lead—if I even take a bite of things like that, I start worrying right away. Almost instantly. It’s not just a passing thought; it’s this intense, immediate panic that I’ll gain weight. 

And it's not just about the number on a scale, it's about what that weight represents to me. It represents a total loss of control. I have worked so incredibly hard, day in and day out, to build this discipline. I’ve fine-tuned my body to be this perfectly calibrated tool for my woodworking. If I let that heavy food in, if I give in to that sort of mindless consumption, I just know I'll gain weight and lose the grip I’ve worked so hard to keep. 

It’s like... well, think about a beautifully restored antique clock. You wouldn't just pour thick, cheap oil into the delicate gears and expect it to keep perfect time, would you? You’d ruin the mechanism. You’d lose all that meticulous fine-tuning. That’s exactly how I feel about my body and my routine. The second I even think about eating those heavy meals, I can feel that grip slipping, and I just can't allow that to happen. I've spent years getting my life and my body perfectly streamlined. So yes, I maintain my intake very, very carefully, because the alternative—that constant worry, that fear of gaining weight and losing my edge—it's just completely unacceptable to me. I simply won't let it happen.
Do you feel that your eating habits are more about avoiding weight gain or about maintaining the physical and mental efficiency you need for your work?

Well, it’s... it’s really both, isn't it? Or rather, one completely feeds into the other, and people just don't seem to grasp that connection. 

I mean, I know why I'm sitting here talking to you right now. My regular doctor sent me here specifically because my weight has dropped so low recently, and now suddenly everyone is making this absolute, monumental fuss about it. He looked at the scale at my last check-up and just started in with the lectures, and of course my husband heard about it, and now it's just this endless chorus of panic from everyone around me. They act like it's some sort of terrible crisis. 

But from my perspective? From the inside looking out? They just don't understand the physical mechanics of my day-to-day life. I honestly feel like being this light is exactly what helps me keep up with the shop. When you are fifty-nine years old and you are spending ten, twelve hours a day on your feet, maneuvering around the band saw, dodging clamps, and leaning over massive workbenches... you cannot afford to carry around extra bulk. You just can't. 

If I were heavier, if I put on the weight that my doctor and my husband seem so desperate for me to have, I would absolutely get slowed down. I'd be sluggish. I wouldn't be able to pivot or bend or stay as agile as I need to be. So when you ask if it's about avoiding the weight or maintaining the efficiency... the low weight *is* the efficiency. They look at me and see a number on a chart that they don't like, but I look at myself and I see a machine that is perfectly streamlined. Being this light means I don't get bogged down. I can glide through a crowded workspace, I can work for hours without feeling heavy or lethargic, and I can maintain my absolute focus. The fuss they make is just so entirely disproportionate to the reality of how well I'm functioning, because honestly, keeping the weight off is the only way I can maintain the pace my work demands.
Are there any other aspects of your daily routine, beyond work and social events, that you feel are being impacted by your efforts to maintain your current weight?

Well, impacted... I mean, if you want to talk about things being impacted, it’s not really my efforts that are the problem, it’s everyone else’s reaction to them. Because, yes, I still go to the shop every single day. I’m there before the sun is even fully up, just like I always have been. It’s my shop, I built that business from nothing, and I know every inch of it. 

But lately... well, it’s become incredibly frustrating. My husband, and now even the two apprentices I hired last spring—good kids, but they just hover constantly now—they’ve started taking over all the heavier work. And I don't just mean offering a hand here and there. I mean, if a delivery of solid oak or thick maple slabs comes in, they practically sprint to the loading dock before I can even set my thermos down. They won't let me lift the large planks onto the jointer anymore. 

And my husband will just show up in the middle of the afternoon, completely unannounced, supposedly just to say hello, but I know exactly what he’s doing. He’s checking on me. He’ll stand there and insist on moving the heavy sheets of plywood himself, or he’ll pull one of the apprentices aside and whisper something, and then suddenly they're all watching me like hawks. It’s... it just disrupts my entire flow. I tell them I’m perfectly fine, that I’ve been hauling lumber for decades, but they just give each other these *looks*. Every time I reach for a heavy pipe clamp or try to load the thickness planer, someone is suddenly right there, gently taking it out of my hands. 

It honestly makes the whole place feel less like my own. It used to be my sanctuary, my perfectly controlled environment where I was the one in charge of every movement. And now I have these watchdogs constantly stepping in, treating me like I’m made of spun glass. So, yes, my daily routine is definitely impacted, but mostly because I’m not allowed to just exist in my own workspace without an audience second-guessing my stamina.
Do you feel like your fear of gaining weight is affecting your overall quality of life?

Well, "quality of life" is such a subjective term, isn't it? If you're asking if my routine makes me unhappy, absolutely not. I thrive on it. The only thing—and I mean the *only* thing—that brings down my quality of life right now is this constant, suffocating scrutiny from everyone else. 

Like I was just saying about the shop... my husband and the apprentices, they just will not let it go. They keep saying I look too thin. My husband actually sat me down the other night, right in the middle of me trying to sketch out a new cabinetry commission, and he had this awful, pitying look on his face, telling me I look frail. Frail! I've been sanding and finishing solid oak all week, there is nothing frail about me. And the apprentices, they whisper when they think I can't hear them, looking at my arms, making these little comments to each other about how I'm supposedly wasting away.
